card.hook: Most squares make you squeeze into a corner to fit everything in. Deera Square gives you a huge paved space to step back in, with fountains up front and a big mosque rising behind them.
card.stand_here: Stand about 240 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. You'll be looking across Deera Square at the Imam Turki bin Abdullah Grand Mosque.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the paving, fountains and mosque all in one shot. Try zoom 0.5x for more fountains in the foreground, then zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for details of the mosque.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the mosque on the upper third line with fountains and paving below, then tap the mosque and slide a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go in the early evening around golden hour, when the mosque and the paving glow warmly. Wait a moment and people will walk through the frame and add some life.
card.selfie_here: Stand next to one of the square's three fountains with the open square behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone a little higher.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand in the open part of the square facing the mosque, so the whole square and the mosque fit in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos for personal use are generally fine, but be respectful when people are in your shot. Keep the palace and government buildings out of your frame, as they shouldn't be photographed.
card.challenge: Get the fountains big in the foreground, the mosque in the background, and one stranger walking through the middle, without anyone looking at your phone.
card.good_to_know: Deera Square is also called Justice Square or Safa Square, and its Arabic name is Sāḥat ad-Dayrah. It sits in the old heart of Riyadh, in the Qasr al-Hukm District next to the al-Hukm Palace compound. For an old-meets-new second shot, Al Masmak Fort's mud-brick walls and watchtowers are at the square's edge. It's closed on Fridays, so check the official site for its hours first.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 240 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. You'll be looking across Deera Square at the Imam Turki bin Abdullah Grand Mosque.

card.hook: Picture yourself on a glass-sided bridge about 300 metres above Riyadh, with the whole city laid out below and the tower's giant arch over your head. Locals call that arch the "bottle opener", and you'll be standing inside it.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject on the Sky Bridge of Kingdom Centre, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Pick a window with a clear view rather than a crowded gap, and face out over the city.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the skyline and the glass bridge together. Go to 0.5x for the widest view, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out single towers and streets far below.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the city and drag the slider down to make it a little darker, so the sunset colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Go just before sunset. You'll catch the sky changing colour and the first city lights coming on.
card.selfie_here: Head to the pedestrian walkway across from Olaya Street and put the tower behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold your phone a little low so the building rises over your shoulder. Check the exact spot on the map, as it's only given by street name.
card.ask_someone: Stand at the corner where King Fahad Road meets Olaya Street (or 200-500 m south along King Fahad Road) and ask a passer-by to frame you with the tower behind.
card.rules_and_safety: One visitor review says cameras aren't allowed on the Sky Bridge but phones are fine. Check the official site for current rules. The bridge is about 300 metres up, so take it easy if heights aren't your thing.
card.challenge: Catch the glass without catching your own reflection: press your phone gently against the window, shade it with your hand, and see how clean a shot you can get.
card.good_to_know: Kingdom Centre is a 99-storey tower, about 302 m tall, finished in 2002. Its almond-shaped body is topped by that huge inverted arch, with a glass-sided skybridge across the opening. Lower down you'll find offices, a hotel, apartments and the Al-Mamlaka shopping mall.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject on the Sky Bridge of Kingdom Centre, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Pick a window with a clear view rather than a crowded gap, and face out over the city.

card.hook: Picture a golden ball balanced on top of a slim tower, with Riyadh traffic humming past below. You can't really miss it, and it makes a great photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on King Fahad Road, back at pavement level so the whole tower fits in. Turn north-west and hold your phone upright.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole tower with a bit of sky around it. If the golden sphere looks small, tap zoom 2x. Only use zoom 0.5x if you're close, and keep the tower in the middle of the screen, because it leans and stretches near the edges.
card.make_it_pop: After dark, tap the lit sphere, then slide the brightness down a little so it keeps its detail instead of turning into a white blob.
card.best_time: Come at sunset or after dark, when the sphere is lit. Sunset is around 5:15 pm in winter and 6:30 pm in summer, so arrive about 20 minutes early to try different angles in the fading light.
card.selfie_here: Olaya Street is where the golden globe gets its cleanest light around golden hour, so try your selfie there. Use the front camera and keep the tower over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On the King Fahad Road side of the tower, ask a passer-by to frame you with the full tower behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the pavement and well back from the traffic when you stop to shoot. If you go up to The Globe restaurant, keep photo-taking brief so other diners aren't disturbed. Going up inside may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Line the tower up with a vertical gridline, wait for a gap in the traffic, and take one portrait-format shot where the sphere sits clear of lamp posts and signs.
card.good_to_know: Al Faisaliah Tower is 267 metres high and was designed by Foster + Partners. It was completed in 2000 and was the first skyscraper built in Saudi Arabia. The golden sphere gives it the nickname Star Dome, and it's named after King Faisal bin Abdulaziz.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on King Fahad Road, back at pavement level so the whole tower fits in. Turn north-west and hold your phone upright.

card.hook: Picture a sand dune that someone built a museum out of. That's the National Museum of Saudi Arabia, and its soft curve and warm sandy colours look great on a phone.
card.stand_here: Walk out to the Murabba' Square side of the National Museum, where the curved west facade is. The phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the building and step back until the whole curve fits on your screen.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to catch the long curve of the facade. Then switch to 1x for a natural view of one section, and try 2x or 5x (if your phone has them) for the wall texture and entrance.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the facade, then drag the slider to make the picture a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out and the sandy colour stays rich.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is usually best for the west facade, because the low sun warms the sandy tones. Early morning is calmer, with fewer people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Try the small hill in the lawned park at the back of the museum, under the shade trees, or the courtyard garden along the palm-lined walkways. Use the front camera (0.5x if yours has it) and check on arrival that the museum is over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a few steps back from the museum's front facade, so the whole exterior fits in the frame against the Riyadh skyline, while you pose in front of the building.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos are generally fine in most areas inside, but watch for 'no flash' or 'no photography' signs in sensitive exhibits. Access can vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole curve, then one close-up with a person walking past, so we can see how big the building really is.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened in 1999 as part of the King Abdulaziz Historical Centre. Architect Raymond Moriyama took his inspiration from the Red Sands dunes just outside Riyadh, and the layout forms a crescent pointing towards Mecca. It's about 369 m across, with eight galleries inside that run from the geology of Arabia to the Unification.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk out to the Murabba' Square side of the National Museum, where the curved west facade is. The phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the building and step back until the whole curve fits on your screen.
